recognition.quote: Awarded 3rd Place at the ICHARMM-2025 SE Poster Presentation for applied AI research on SkinGuard AI — a clinical melanoma screening system built to run fully offline.
SkinGuard AI achieved 0.9395 ROC-AUC and an Expected Calibration Error of 0.0072 — independently verified on its live, public results page.

story.headline: I don't ship a model that only performs well on paper.
paragraphs: I started my B.S. in Software Engineering at CECOS University in Peshawar without a fixed idea of what kind of engineer I wanted to be. That changed during my Final Year Project — an early attempt at a melanoma detection model that, honestly, wasn't very good. It worked on paper, on a clean validation set, and fell apart on anything realistic.

Fixing that became the project. Across eight iterations, I rebuilt the training data, closed a class-imbalance gap, and eventually discovered something most published melanoma classifiers never check for: a massive accuracy collapse when a dermoscopy-trained model sees an ordinary phone photo instead. Solving that — not just training a bigger model — is what SkinGuard AI actually is.

That experience set the standard I hold every project to now. A model that performs well in a notebook is a start, not a result. I want to know how it fails, whether it knows when it's uncertain, and whether it still works when the network doesn't. That question is the thread running through everything I've built since — an on-device security system with 397 automated tests, a RAG pipeline that cites its sources instead of guessing, and a multi-agent system hardened against the exact attacks that break unguarded ones.
My mission is straightforward: build AI that works reliably in the conditions that actually matter — offline, resource-constrained, and high-stakes — not just in a polished demo.
story.differentiator: What makes me different is that I audit my own results before I trust them, and I document what fails as carefully as what succeeds.
